item.title: Self-Supervised Tuning of Low-Fidelity Optimization Models via High-Fidelity Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2610.28851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-fidelity (LF) optimization models are widely used in large-scale operations because they can be solved efficiently and reliably, but they often exhibit systematic errors relative to high-fidelity (HF) formulations that better capture physical and operational constraints. Existing learning-based approaches typically rely on supervised or semi-supervised training with HF solutions, which are expensive to compute and may not align with HF operational objectives. We propose a self-supervised framework that parameterizes LF optimization models directly from HF feedback. The low-fidelity problem is embedded as a differentiable optimization layer and trained end-to-end, while a HF correction problem evaluates its solution and provides gradient information through its dual variables, without requiring HF solution labels. We evaluate the framework on optimal power flow, optimal gas flow, and pooling problems, spanning different sources of low- and high-fidelity mismatch. Across all three applications, the self-supervised approach improves objective quality and feasibility over untuned LF models and generally outperforms semi-supervised training. The learned parameterizations also generalize to unseen operating conditions and, for network applications with up to 30,000 nodes, to systems not encountered during training.
item.dc:creator: Gonzalo E. Constante-Flores, Andr\'e H. Quisaguano-Paredes, Asha Ramanujam, Rishabh Gupta, Can Li

item.title: Physics-Informed Mixed Integer Programming Methods for Optimal Patch Antennas
item.description: arXiv:2610.28879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Antennas come in various shapes and sizes, as their performance characteristics are very much dependent on their exact shape. Coming up with a shape that matches desired design characteristics has, up until this moment, been largely the domain of metaheuristics and local optimization methods. While these methods are convenient, they generally provide no performance guarantees and rarely allow to enforce hard design constraints. In this paper, we show how Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) can be used to optimize the shape of so-called patch antennas. The methodological focus is to show how underlying laws of physics allow to derive effective bounds on variables as well as new cutting planes. These greatly improve the effectiveness of the underlying basic MIP model, enabling the automated design of practically relevant patch antennas for a wide variety of applications.
item.dc:creator: Ruben Hoeksma, Jesse van Rhijn, Marc Uetz, Wick Wijnholds

item.title: Optimal Dividends and Proactive Capital Injection over a Finite Horizon
item.description: arXiv:2610.29085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a finite-horizon dividend and capital-injection problem for a Brownian surplus process with time-varying financing costs. Under a classical passive-injection policy, capital is supplied only at the solvency boundary. Anticipated increases in financing costs may instead make it optimal to inject capital while reserves remain strictly positive. We characterize this proactive financing mechanism through an auxiliary Dynkin game for the marginal value of liquidity. The game identifies an endogenous lower financing boundary and an upper dividend boundary, and yields restrictions on intervention timing and comparative statics with respect to the financing-cost path. Under a regular intervention-band condition, we recover the control value by spatial integration of the game value and verify that the optimal policy is two-sided reflection between the two boundaries. We establish this condition for a canonical class with decreasing marginal dividend rewards, increasing marginal financing costs, and a compatible piecewise affine terminal marginal value. Strictly decreasing financing costs eliminate positive-reserve financing contact and reduce the marginal game to a one-player stopping problem. Numerical examples illustrate the optimal policies and the effects of anticipated financing conditions on shareholder value and intervention thresholds.
item.dc:creator: Ran Xu, Zuo Quan Xu, Xueying Zhang

item.title: Partially Observed McKean--Vlasov Control with Vanishing Observation Intensities
item.description: arXiv:2610.29133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study partially observed McKean--Vlasov jump-diffusions with controlled counting intensities that may vanish and depend on the unconditional physical state distribution. A deterministic upper bound on the likelihood supports one-sided state--likelihood variations, a smooth-test-function expansion of the physical state marginal, and a necessary maximum principle without inverse intensity or likelihood terms. We also establish a one-sided total-variation derivative of the physical probability on the fixed noise space, including a nonnegative singular component on baseline-null histories. A quadratic example shows, within a specified policy family and under explicit conditions, that positive variance feedback raises the first-order activation fee threshold while negative feedback lowers it.
item.dc:creator: Jie Xiong, Ying Yang

item.title: ORSMT: Unleashing the Potential of Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Semantic Verification and Repair in LLM-Based Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.29145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models increasingly automate optimization modeling from natural language problems, producing written mathematics, solver code and a returned report. Verifying one optimization problem across these artifacts requires semantic comparison: unequal models can attain the same objective, equivalent models can use different auxiliary variables, and mutually consistent artifacts can omit the same source requirement. ORSMT provides a typed semantic interface and exact SMT relation queries. It aligns observable decisions, projects auxiliary variables, proves or refutes feasible region and objective relations, localizes refutations to implicated rows or domains and links source texts when available. It then reconstructs one artifact from another, and each adopted candidate passes the required relation checks. Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, ORSMT improves the model-code match rate in all 72 benchmark and generator combinations before selection. Protected selection raises the aggregate rate from 43.2% to 88.2% and the share that are both correct and matched from 25.2% to 40.2%. On the 1,905 refuted outputs, certified voting under the shared fallback makes 50.9% of outputs correct and matched, compared with 44.8% for ReLoop and 49.4% for Opt-Verifier. A separate one-round source revision followed by exact reconstruction restores a model-code match for 84.4% of the refuted pairs.
item.dc:creator: Rui Zhang, Chenyu Zhou, Jianghao Lin, Yaoxin Wu, Dongdong Ge, Wen Song

item.title: A Link-Based Algorithm for Stochastic User Equilibrium with Bounded Choice and Local Detour Threshold
item.description: arXiv:2610.29151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study develops a novel solution method for stochastic user equilibrium (SUE) under the bounded choice model with local detour threshold (BCM-LDT SUE; Rasmussen et al., 2024), which restricts the choice set in line with observed route choice behavior. The model assigns zero probability to paths whose total cost exceeds a bound or whose local detour exceeds a threshold; thus, the path choice set varies with link costs. The proposed algorithm updates link flows while implicitly enumerating the path choice set via a depth-first search (DFS) pruned with the BCM-LDT bounds. This distinguishes it from the original algorithm, which updates path flows, and enables quasi-Newton-type acceleration. Since paths are never stored, the method can handle choice sets totaling on the order of $10^7$ paths. On a personal computer, it reached equilibrium in a few to about fifteen minutes, not only for the Anaheim network under the original settings but also for larger networks such as Winnipeg and Barcelona.
item.dc:creator: Takeshi Nagae

item.title: A Shadow Sequence Technique for Last-Iterate Convergence Analysis of the Random Reshuffling Method: Relaxed Stepsize Conditions and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2610.29166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove two last-iterate convergence bounds of the random reshuffling (RR) method in the smooth general convex finite-sum optimization. In the proved results, the stepsize sequence $\{\eta_{k}\}_{k}$ of RR is an arbitrary positive non-increasing sequence with $\eta_{1}\lesssim 1/(\operatorname{polylog}(n)L)$, where $n$ is the number of components of the finite-sum objective and $L$ is the smoothness parameter. Specifically, a last-iterate convergence rate $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{\Vert x_{1}^{1}-x_{*}\Vert^2}{n\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}}+\sigma_{*}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\eta_{k}^{2}}{\sum_{l=k}^{K}\eta_{l}}\right)$ of RR is proved, where $x_{*}$ is a solution of the optimization problem and $\sigma_{*}^{2}$ is the variance at the solution $x_{*}$. This rate is novel to the last-iterate of RR. Also, a last-iterate convergence rate $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\frac{\Vert x_{1}^{1}-x_{*}\Vert^2}{n\sum_{k=1}^{K}\eta_{k}}+n\sigma_{*}^{2}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\eta_{k}^{3}}{\sum_{l=k}^{K}\eta_{l}} \right)$ of RR is proved. A similar rate exists in the literature, but only under a restrictive stepsize condition $\eta\lesssim 1/(n L)$ and does not allow varying stepsizes. At the heart of our proof for the latter rate is an auxiliary sequence named the shadow sequence, which has the same epoch endpoints with the iterate sequence generated by RR. The shadow sequence can be regarded as an iterate sequence generated by performing an inexact RR on an auxiliary interpolated problem or performing a novel variant of random reshuffled SVRG on the original problem. The shadow sequence technique sheds light on deeper understanding of RR and may be useful in the analysis of other shuffling methods.
item.dc:creator: Hai Liu, Tiande Guo, Congying Han

item.title: Curvature-Scaled Sharpness-Aware Minimization: Convergence Beyond Smoothness
item.description: arXiv:2610.29192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has established itself as a widely used method for training deep neural networks. Despite its popularity, existing convergence guarantees for SAM-type methods require smoothness, a restrictive assumption. Generalized smoothness conditions have recently been proposed in the analysis of gradient methods but remain underexplored for SAM. To analyze the effect of SAM's perturbation under generalized smoothness, we use relative gradient distortion to quantify how the sharpness-aware direction departs from the original gradient. Under $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness, we show that this distortion can become unbounded near stationarity for SAM and at large gradients for its unnormalized variant (USAM), with examples where SAM cycles and USAM diverges. We then establish a necessary condition for uniform distortion control among perturbations along the gradient whose nonnegative multipliers depend only on its norm. Motivated by this condition, we propose Curvature-Scaled SAM (CS-SAM), which scales both the perturbation and the descent step by suitable curvature upper bounds, and prove that it uniformly bounds the distortion. Under both $(L_0,L_1)$- and $(H_0,H_1)$-smoothness, we establish deterministic $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the best squared gradient norm on nonconvex objectives, last-iterate $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the function gap on convex objectives with a minimizer, and linear convergence under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. With zero perturbation, our guarantees recover the rates for gradient descent with $(L_0,L_1)$- or $(H_0,H_1)$-based step-sizes. Minibatch experiments on computer vision tasks demonstrate competitive performance for both variants, with the $(H_0,H_1)$ variant achieving the highest mean best-test accuracy in all four settings against tuned SAM and USAM with constant and cosine annealing schedules.
item.dc:creator: Dimitris Oikonomou, Nicolas Loizou

item.title: Group Distributionally Robust Optimization over Decentralized Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.29261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study group distributionally robust optimization (GDRO) over decentralized networks, where workers collaborate to learn robust models by minimizing the maximum local risk. Existing methods optimize only dual-regularized surrogates and establish guarantees for a globally averaged model that is not available to workers. In this paper, we directly optimize the original GDRO objective and establish guarantees for local models in semi-decentralized (SemiDec) and fully decentralized (Dec) settings. A key difficulty is that applying the primal-dual decomposition from centralized GDRO yields worker-dependent losses whose evaluation requires unavailable cross-worker information. To address this challenge, we develop a novel error decomposition that recasts decentralized GDRO as (i) a decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) problem and a prediction-with-expert-advice problem in SemiDec, and as (ii) two coupled D-OCO problems in Dec, with discrepancy terms capturing inconsistencies among local decisions. By isolating consensus errors in analysis, we develop modular frameworks that support different consensus routines. We then establish the \emph{first} per-worker convergence guarantees for optimizing the original GDRO objective over decentralized networks. Instantiations with accelerated gossip and Choco-gossip achieve an $O(\sqrt{(\log m)/T})$ convergence rate over $T$ update rounds, while experiments demonstrate improved worst-worker performance over baselines.
item.dc:creator: Haomin Bai, Junyan Sun, Quan Cheng, Yuanyu Wan, Lijun Zhang

item.title: Adaptive Grid Refinement for Optimal Feedback Control
item.description: arXiv:2610.29368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces an algorithmic approach for adaptive grid refinement for solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) partial differential equation (PDE) to obtain the optimal feedback control. Traditional grid generation methods often face challenges associated with state-space dimensionality, solution regularity, and large variations in the solution. Whereas fixed grid generation methods may fail to capture the intricate details of the optimal solution, our methodology addresses this challenge by dynamically refining the grid used to solve the HJB equation, thereby optimizing computational resource usage while targeting improved solution accuracy. The reinforcement learning (RL)-based approach presented in this study seeks to reduce the node population while constructing a grid with higher node density in regions with large discretization error.
item.dc:creator: Alen E. Golpashin, Matthew T. Clark, Bruce A. Conway

item.title: Local Lyapunov Exponent-Guided Stochastic Midcourse Correction Design of Low-Energy Earth-Moon Transfers
item.description: arXiv:2610.29390v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Midcourse correction is essential for reliable cislunar transfer missions. For low-energy Earth-Moon transfers, strongly nonuniform error growth makes conventional correction strategies less effective. This paper proposes a stochastic midcourse correction design for low-energy Earth-Moon transfers based on local Lyapunov exponent (LLE). The local error-amplification characteristics of the nominal trajectory are first analyzed using an instantaneous LLE. The analysis shows that strong sensitivity is concentrated near periapsis, and that the LLE maxima coincide with regions of strong finite-time error growth. These maxima are therefore used to segment the trajectory and define the number of corrections. Based on this segmentation, a reduced parameterization is introduced to describe the correction epochs, while second-order state transition tensors (STTs) are employed for nonlinear correction targeting. The resulting timing variables are then optimized through a sample-average approximation of the chance-constrained stochastic problem. Paired Monte Carlo simulations show that, under the same mission-accuracy requirements, the proposed strategy greatly improves the reliability and robustness of trajectory recovery while requiring less correction cost than the classical Breakwell spacing-ratio strategy.
item.dc:creator: Zihang Wang, Shuyue Fu, Di Wu, Shengping Gong

item.title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for optimal control of coupled forward-backward stochastic control systems driven by G-Brownian motion
item.description: arXiv:2610.29494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study a coupled forward-backward stochastic control system driven by G-Brownian motion. Based on some detailed estimates for control system, we obtain the variational inequality for cost functional, which is a necessary condition for optimality. Furthermore, we prove that this necessary condition is also a sufficient condition under the usual convexity assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Xiaojuan Li, Mingshang Hu

item.title: Algorithm duality from resolvent Moreau identities
item.description: arXiv:2610.29548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Duality is classically defined as a relationship between objective functions, one that breaks down beyond convexity. We show that a more fundamental duality persists between the resolvent operators used to solve associated problems. We establish a framework from which we obtain complete characterizations of the duality-like correspondences between proximal fixed-point iterations and their alternating minimization scheme counterparts. Namely, we show the known primal-dual relationships between forward--backward splitting and Tseng's alternating minimization algorithm, and between the Douglas-Rachford method and alternating direction method of multipliers, to hold generically and irrespective of problem assumptions. The approach considered herein avoids the machinery of convex analysis entirely, providing a definitive formulation of algorithmic dualities in maximal generality while greatly simplifying their proofs. In particular, assumptions such as monotonicity, weak monotonicity, Lipschitz continuity, and injectivity of linear operators are all shown to be unnecessary. In addition, we utilize our framework to reveal and analyze a novel primal-dual relationship between backward-backward splitting and a special instance of the alternating minimization algorithm. This illustrates how our duality framework provides a principled basis for primal-dual algorithm design and analysis in nonmonotone settings. Finally, our experiments show that our backward--backward splitting--based approach reliably outperforms the FISTA and SR3 algorithms for the LASSO problem.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Calcan, Alberto De Marchi, Scott B. Lindstrom

item.title: Data-driven calibration of a two-dimensional traffic flow model: Dimension reduction and optimization strategies
item.description: arXiv:2610.29557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the data-driven calibration of a two-dimensional first-order macroscopic traffic flow model, in which the movement along and across the road is described by a three-parameter flux model. The calibration is based on three real-world datasets, ranging from microscopic drone trajectories on German highways to aggregated urban sensor measurements. We recall the well-posedness of the underlying scalar conservation law and derive structural properties of the flux model. In particular, one parameter enters linearly and can be eliminated analytically, which reduces the non-linear least-squares problem from three to two dimensions. We solve the full and reduced calibration problem with two local optimization methods, Nelder-Mead and L-BFGS-B, and three global population-based methods Differential Evolution, Consensus-Based Optimization, and its deterministic variant Quasi-Monte Carlo consensus based optimization. In addition to accuracy and computational cost, we examine how sensitive the objective is to the parameters and how robust the algorithms are with respect to randomness and initialization. The reduced formulation is considerably cheaper and less sensitive to the choice of optimizer. The local methods are the most efficient when suitably initialized, whereas the global methods are more robust.
item.dc:creator: Simone G\"ottlich, Jacob Heieck

item.title: A short proof of a range-relative FPTAS for polynomial integer optimization over bounded polyhedra
item.description: arXiv:2610.29573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a short proof of a fully polynomial-time range-relative approximation scheme for polynomial optimization over the integer points of a bounded rational polyhedron in fixed dimension. The proof combines the reflecting-set decomposition of Cook, Hartmann, Kannan, and McDiarmid with Markov's polynomial derivative inequality and uses one integer linear feasibility query per refined cell. The running time is polynomial in the input encoding size, numerical degree, and reciprocal accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Robert Hildebrand

item.title: Accelerated primal-dual dynamics and algorithms for strongly convex-concave bilinear saddle point problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.29723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we develop accelerated primal-dual dynamics and algorithms for strongly convex-concave saddle point problems with bilinear coupling. Combining strongly convex Nesterov dynamics with scaled heavy-ball dynamics, we propose a second-order primal-dual dynamical system with constant damping and derive an associated algorithm by time discretization and coefficient adjustment. Under suitable conditions on the continuous scaling function $\beta(t)$ and the discrete scaling sequence $\beta_k$, we establish primal-dual gap estimates of $\mathcal O(1/\beta(t))$ in continuous time and $\mathcal O(1/\beta_k)$ in discrete time. The maximal admissible growth rates of these scales recover the exponential and linear convergence rates of strongly convex Nesterov methods in continuous and discrete time, respectively. We also prove convergence of the primal-dual trajectory and sequence, even when the dual solution is nonunique. Saddle residual estimates of $\mathcal O(1/\sqrt{\beta(t)})$ and $\mathcal O(1/\sqrt{\beta_k})$ hold under globally Lipschitz gradients in continuous time and with a possibly nonsmooth dual potential in discrete time. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical results and the performance of the proposed methods.
item.dc:creator: Yun-xi Zhang, Yi-bin Xiao, Xin He

item.title: Model Predictive Control: Systematic Design Tailored to Nonholonomic Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.29728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonholonomic systems are ubiquitous in applications such as transportation and robotics, yet their control remains challenging. In order to achieve asymptotic stability of a desired equilibrium, model predictive control (MPC) schemes without stabilizing terminal conditions have recently been proposed for nonholonomic kinematic systems. However, this approach still required lengthy system-specific calculations. This paper eliminates the need for these auxiliary calculations, as we propose a streamlined systematic design for MPC stage costs tailored to nonholonomic systems, utilizing the concepts of privileged coordinates and nonholonomic weights. Furthermore, the proposed design methodology is extended beyond purely kinematic models to a wider class of systems with non-negligible dynamics, and we highlight the geometric meaning of the resulting MPC stage costs. The systematic procedure is demonstrated using an articulated vehicle as an example.
item.dc:creator: Emilia F. P. item.title: Observability Inequality for a Multi-Dimensional Degenerate Schr\"odinger Equation with an Interior Degeneracy Point
item.description: arXiv:2610.29897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the observability inequality for a multi-dimensional degenerate Schr\"odinger equation possessing an interior degeneracy point, where the principal coefficient vanishes at the origin inside the domain and breaks ellipticity. Within a weighted Sobolev space, we establish the spectral properties, well-posedness, and regularity estimates for the degenerate operator. To tackle the failure of classical controllability tools, we develop a regularization approximation scheme. We construct a sequence of non-degenerate approximating problems. We then establish uniform a-priori estimates and solution convergence. Furthermore, we derive an observability inequality for the regularized problems and pass to the limit. This yields a non-standard observability inequality for the original degenerate equation for sufficiently large observation time, which quantifies the influence of the degeneracy strength on the observation time. Crucially, we establish the precise parameter restriction $3\alpha + N > 4$ to ensure that every test function in $C_0^\infty(\Omega)$ belongs to $D(\mathcal A^{\frac 32})$.
item.dc:creator: Dong-Hui Yang, Ghadir Shokor, Mengze Gu, Jie Zhong

item.title: Reinforcement Learning for Global-Local Control of Dynamic Networks with Applications to Systemic Risk
item.description: arXiv:2610.29906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a reinforcement learning framework for solving control problems on dynamic networks, where control decisions consist of a combination of graph-level (global) and node-level (local) actions. To exploit the underlying network structure in a policy-gradient algorithm, we introduce a message-passing neural network architecture with separate global and local policy heads. The architecture ensures that the resulting policies satisfy natural permutation symmetries and transparency constraints. Our main theoretical contribution is an analysis of the robustness and regularity properties of the proposed architecture. We derive explicit Lipschitz bounds with respect to both parameter and input perturbations and use these estimates to establish convergence guarantees for a projected policy-gradient algorithm. The resulting constants reveal how architectural choices and graph characteristics influence sensitivity to input perturbations and the convergence behavior of gradient-based optimization methods. As an application, we study the management of systemic risk in financial networks, where a regulator allocates capital interventions across interconnected institutions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed reinforcement learning architecture outperforms standard architectures based on feedforward neural networks while the learned policies fulfill desirable symmetry and transparency constraints. The algorithm scales to large networks and effectively combines global budget decisions with local allocation policies by exploiting the underlying graph structure.
item.dc:creator: Nils Detering, Florian Grell, Thilo Meyer-Brandis

item.title: Worst-Case Finite-Horizon Analysis of Perturbed LQR via Performance Estimation Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.29910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an exact formulation to quantify the finite-horizon robustness of a Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) subject to norm-bounded Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) parametric uncertainties, using the Performance Estimation Problem (PEP) framework. Originally developed for optimization, this method allows us to reformulate the worst-case performance search as a rank-constrained Semidefinite Program (SDP). By applying operator interpolation, this formulation retains the sequence variables, allowing the worst-case to be explicitly reconstructed when a rank-one solution is found. This approach also opens new possibilities for the finite-horizon certification of broader system classes, such as data-driven models or nonlinear components. Using this framework, we observe that finite-horizon LTI perturbations do not simply follow asymptotic strategies. Instead, they align slowly decaying invariant manifolds with specific initial conditions to drive transient growth, causing a bifurcation in the worst-case behavior as the horizon length changes. Finally, we show numerically that our performance bounds sit between the upper bounds of Integral Quadratic Constraint (IQC) relaxations and a lower bound derived from a pseudospectral heuristic.
item.dc:creator: Anthony Couthures, Gianluca Bianchin, Julien M. Hendrickx

item.title: Small-time approximate controllability of bilinear Schr\"odinger equations on compact normal homogeneous spaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.29940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove small-time global approximate controllability in $L^2$ for bilinear Schr\"odinger equations on compact connected normal homogeneous spaces. The controls act through finitely many smooth real-valued potentials. We first construct finite saturating families on compact connected Lie groups endowed with bi-invariant metrics, using Peter-Weyl theory and the Casimir operator. Their phase saturation contains the representative algebra and is therefore dense in $L^2$. We extend this construction to normal homogeneous quotients using finite generation of the algebra of highest-weight functions. Global controllability follows by combining the phase-to-gradient transport argument of [8] with the gradient generation theorem of [23] and Moser's transport of positive densities.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Parada

item.title: Dual Effect and Certainty Equivalence Revisited for a Linear-Gaussian Dual Control Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.30034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper revisits the relation between dual effect and certainty equivalence (CE) through a scalar linear-Gaussian model. In dual control, the current input affects not only the immediate cost but also the information available for future decisions, and hence the future cost. Dynamic programming (DP) provides a natural framework for formulating dual control problems. At each step of the Bellman recursion, an optimal input minimizes the sum of the stage cost and the expected cost-to-go. We restrict attention to stage costs minimized by the CE input. However, CE may not minimize the Bellman objective because of the input-dependent expected cost-to-go. Classical no-dualeffect (NDE) conditions guarantee CE optimality in certain problem classes by requiring the conditional distribution of the estimation error to be independent of past controls. In the present model, we observe that CE can remain optimal at the level of a single Bellman recursion even when the classical NDE conditions fail, provided that the expected cost-to-go is independent of the current input. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a notion of NDE formulated directly at the level of the Bellman objective, which we call Bellman-side NDE. Under some mild regularity conditions, we show that Bellman-side NDE can be characterized by a heat equation. This characterization identifies the class of Bellman-side NDE functions, and further yields a decomposition of a generic cost-to-go function into a Bellman-side NDE component and a dual-effect component.
item.dc:creator: Ying Wang, Yue Ju, H{\aa}kan Hjalmarsson

item.title: Borrowing Strength Across Stores: Transfer Learning for Choice-Based Revenue Management
item.description: arXiv:2610.28708v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large retail chains must tailor assortment and pricing decisions to local customer preferences, yet even retailers with extensive sales records often have limited data for estimating demand at the store or local market level, particularly in product categories with short selling windows. Local estimation (fitting a demand model for each store on its own) can therefore be unreliable, while pooling data across stores improves estimation precision at the cost of ignoring local demand heterogeneity. We study how retailers can balance these competing effects through transfer learning under a multinomial logit (MNL) demand model. We propose a shrinkage estimator that combines store-specific demand estimates with information pooled from other stores. Unlike the linear or quadratic settings underlying much of the existing theoretical literature on information transfer in operations, the nonlinear MNL likelihood does not admit a straightforward bias-variance decomposition. By exploiting its self-concordant-like properties, we establish finite-sample performance guarantees that characterize when information transfer improves demand estimation and how the appropriate degree of shrinkage depends on local sample size, feature dimensionality, and cross-store heterogeneity. We further derive regret bounds for downstream assortment and pricing decisions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the operational benefits of shrinkage across different data environments. An empirical study using data from several hundred stores of a European apparel retailer shows that shrinkage improves out-of-sample product prioritization and revenue capture relative to both local estimation and full pooling. Our findings demonstrate how retailers can leverage information across their store networks to improve revenue management decisions while preserving local demand differences.
item.dc:creator: Recep Yusuf Bekci, Stefanus Jasin, Joline Uichanco

item.title: Deflation-Based Spectral Preconditioning for the Conjugate Gradient Method on Perturbed Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.28808v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider sequences of large symmetric positive-definite linear systems in which spectral information from a reference matrix $A$ is reused to accelerate the solution of a nearby system with perturbed matrix $A(t)=A+tE$, where $E$ is symmetric, $\|E\|_F=1$, and $t\geq0$ is the perturbation size. We compare deflated conjugate gradient (deflated CG) with preconditioned CG (PCG) equipped with a scaled spectral preconditioner constructed from the same spectral information of $A$. First, we derive an energy-norm error characterization of deflated CG. We then use perturbation analysis to show that, after one additional PCG iteration, the squared PCG error is bounded, up to terms of order $t^2$, by an explicit multiple of the squared deflated CG error. This result clarifies the role of the scaling parameter in the preconditioner. Experiments show that the scaled spectral preconditioner recovers much of the convergence improvement provided by deflation while requiring fewer products with $A(t)$.
item.dc:creator: Youssef Diouane, Selime G\"urol, Oussama Mouhtal, Dominique Orban

item.title: A Model-Free Continuous-Time RL Algorithm from Discrete-Time Off-Policy Data with End-to-End Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2610.28915v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we study continuous-time reinforcement learning, where the state follows an unknown stochastic differential equation but only a fixed off-policy batch of discrete-time transitions is available. Standard discrete-time Q-learning becomes problematic as the sampling interval shrinks, because differences between action values vanish. Continuous-time alternatives, such as Deep Advantage Updating and martingale q-learning, preserve the action signal but jointly learn a value function and an action-dependent critic. Building on the PhiBE-Q formulation (arXiv:2606.21925), we develop a model-free PhiBE policy iteration (PhiBE-PI) framework that uses a single state-action critic while preserving the continuous-time action-ranking scale. At each iteration, the framework learns the critic directly from sampled increments and uses it to improve the policy. The same batch is reused throughout, without explicitly estimating the drift or diffusion. We further develop an implementation under linear function approximation and establish a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee for the learned policy. Our analysis quantifies how errors from time discretization, function approximation, and finite-sample policy evaluation propagate through policy iteration. It accounts for the dependence of successive policies on the reused data, so the guarantee does not require a fresh batch at each iteration. Moreover, we identify a bias-variance trade-off: smaller sampling intervals improve the approximation to the continuous-time problem but can increase statistical error at a fixed sample size. Thus, finer time discretization does not necessarily lead to better policy performance.
item.dc:creator: Chaorui Yao, Yuming Paul Zhang, Lin Yang, Yuhua Zhu

item.title: Kinetic Mean-Field Planning via Schr\"odinger Bridges: Existence, Penalization, and Consistency Bounds
item.description: arXiv:2610.28924v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a mean-field planning problem for a swarm of interacting, non-cooperative agents whose dynamics are stochastic and kinetic. The noise acts on the velocity only, and the interaction (of Cucker-Smale type for instance) enters through the drift. For a fixed flow, the problem reduces to a Schr\"odinger bridge problem, and we first prove the existence of an equilibrium by a Schauder fixed-point argument. Then we replace the hard terminal constraint by a penalty function and show that equilibria of the penalized problems converge, along subsequences, to an equilibrium of the original problem. Since equilibria are not unique in general, we instead quantify the consistency error, which measures how far an equilibrium of the penalized problem is from being an equilibrium of the original one. The rate is of order $n^{-1/2}$ for the relative-entropy penalty. The proof relies on the quantitative stability of entropic optimal transport and on a pointwise linear growth bound on the score of the degenerate reference dynamics, which is of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Erhan Bayraktar, Zhiyan Ding, Hiroaki Horikawa

item.title: Dynamics of Hidden Learning Structure
item.description: arXiv:2610.29054v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A learner's present predictions do not fully determine how it will learn next. We study the dynamics of hidden learning structure through two related operations. Fiber Regulation Theory (FRT) describes protected repair of existing function and the learning responses left available after repair. Fiber Acquisition Theory (FAT) describes the formation and renewal of trainable structure, distinguishing neutral installation, access to a learning signal, and additional functional directions. The two operations also constrain one another. A repair obligation can force a change in a learning channel, while acquired features can make new protected repairs feasible or reduce the minimum coefficient cost of existing ones. We characterize joint admissibility and response reachability, and give a finite supervised-learning construction in which the two operations together produce a favorable response absent from either operation alone. We implement protected head repair and fixed-capacity LoRA renewal in Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, under replay and output distillation. Across two training trajectories differing in seed and within-task example order, the coordinated policy achieves higher teacher-forced Exact than either separate policy in all four comparisons. It also has the lowest macro NLL under both learning rules on the second trajectory. The implementations realize structure-conditioned self-regulation within specified information and action constraints: accessible state readouts and arrived evidence guide repairs and structural renewals, and ordinary learning continues from the modified state.
item.dc:creator: Qinyou Wang

item.title: The Local Dyadic Conjecture
item.description: arXiv:2610.29197v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A rational with denominator a power of two is said to be dyadic. A long standing conjecture of Paul Seymour predicts that for an ideal clutter, the dual of the set covering problem always admits an optimal solution where all variables take dyadic values. We present a local version of this conjecture, and motivate it by proving an important special case.
item.dc:creator: Mahtab Alghasi, Bertrand Guenin, Levent Tun\c{c}el

item.title: Interpretable Cutting Plane Selection for Mixed-Integer Linear Programming Using Genetic Programming
item.description: arXiv:2610.29311v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cutting planes (cuts) remove fractional solutions from mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs) without excluding any feasible integer solutions, making them a key ingredient in modern MILP solvers. Current state-of-the-art solvers rely on fine-tuned handcrafted cut strategies, which, despite their effectiveness, remain inherently static and can be suboptimal. More recently, learning-based approaches have been proposed to design adaptive cut strategies; however, most of these methods are based on neural networks, offering limited interpretability and providing no guarantees of convergence. In this paper, we propose \emph{Genetic Programming and Statistics-based Cut Selection} (GPSCS), the first learning-based framework that explicitly generalizes handcrafted cut selection heuristics into a fully interpretable policy. First, a genetic programming model evolves a symbolic scoring function that ranks candidate cuts using features derived from the cuts and the solving context. Second, a lightweight statistics-based mechanism adaptively determines the number of top-ranked cuts to add at each separation round by detecting significant score dropouts. We evaluate GPSCS within the SCIP solver on seven classes of synthetic and real-world benchmark instances, with a strong emphasis on generalization: evaluation instances are on average 41 times harder than those used for training. Experimental results show that GPSCS improves average solving time by $6\%$ compared to SCIP's default cut selection strategy and achieves a two-fold speedup over both a recent neural-network-based approach and a no-cut baseline, demonstrating strong robustness and generalization across heterogeneous MILP families.
item.dc:creator: Gwen maudet, Mathis Da Cunha, Gr\'egoire Danoy

item.title: Dissipation Bounds and Hardness in Globally Asymptotically Stable Quadratic Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.29512v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study worst-case finite-time energy dissipation in quadratic systems with proved global asymptotic stability (GAS). Estimating the maximum retained energy fraction to any fixed positive additive error below $1/2$ is NP-hard, even when the input includes a strict quartic Lyapunov function and proof of strictness, both constructed in polynomial time. NP denotes nondeterministic polynomial time. For a partially damped family, the unit-sphere minimum norm of the coupling map equals the structured coefficient distance to loss of GAS. Positive distances at most $1/2$ give two-sided inverse-square halving-time bounds with explicit coefficient factors. Polynomial-factor approximation of the least dissipated fraction, halving time or coefficient distance is NP-hard. Additive hardness persists throughout an explicit coefficient neighborhood and under direct damping with exponential stability, a strict quadratic Lyapunov function and a Hurwitz Jacobian. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, where P denotes deterministic polynomial time, no polynomial-time algorithm attains these guarantees on all inputs.
item.dc:creator: Subhransu S. Bhattacharjee

item.title: Dynamical low-rank approximations for the optimal control of matrix ODEs
item.description: arXiv:2610.29554v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider the open-loop optimal control of a dynamical system whose state is described by a time-dependent matrix $X(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$. Gradient-based optimization methods may incur substantial computational and memory costs, particularly for large-scale systems and fine temporal discretizations. To alleviate this computational burden, we develop a mathematical framework to use Dynamical Low Rank Approximations (DLRA) in optimal control problems. We study two distinct paradigms: the first one, called Optimize-then-Project (OtP), first derives the optimality system and then approximates both the state and adjoint equations using DLRA. The second one, called Project-then-Optimize (PtO), first replaces the state equation with its DLR approximation, and then derives the optimality conditions for the resulting optimization problem. The two approaches differ fundamentally concerning the role of the adjoint variable. In OtP, the adjoint variable evolves on the manifold of fixed rank matrices, whereas in PtO, the adjoint variable belongs to the tangent space to the fixed-rank manifold at the evolving state variable. This latter formulation leads to a covariant ODE describing the dynamics of the adjoint variable as the underlying tangent space evolves in time. For both approaches we establish rigorous error estimates for the approximated gradients, identifying how their accuracy depends on the low-rank approximations of initial and terminal conditions, the components of the state and adjoint vector fields normal to the relevant tangent spaces, the stability properties of the dynamics, and the manifold curvature. PtO further requires tailored time discretization strategies for the adjoint covariant ODE, which we show to be robust against small singular values of the state variable. To illustrate the framework, we apply these methods to the optimal control of a random parabolic PDE.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Carrel, Tommaso Vanzan

item.title: Recovering Plausible Transmission Outage Scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2610.29872v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Expansion planning for extreme weather needs outage scenarios that specify which transmission branches fail. However, public outage records often only report customers without power by county, making it unclear how to exploit this information to create outage scenarios. We propose a method to recover sets of outaged branches that most closely match regional load shed data. This gives us sets of plausible outages for a given hazard event. We formulate a bilevel problem with a load shedding DC optimal power flow in the lower level. We relax the binary branch states to differentiate the lower level problem, replace it with its sensitivity matrix, and use gradient descent to update the upper level. We treat the relaxed branch states as probabilities and perform randomized rounding to restore integrality. On three test systems with synthetic outages, the recovered sets reduce the load shed error to $0.02-4.5\%$. On the California Test System with storm data from December 2025, the error falls to $23\%$. These scenarios give expansion planning a reliable source of outage data tied to observed hazards.
item.dc:creator: Karen Ji, Cameron Khanpour, Samuel Talkington, J. Kyle Skolfield, Daniel K. Molzahn

item.title: Saturation on compact manifolds via Stone-Weierstrass type theorem, and forced nonlinear PDEs
item.description: arXiv:2610.29914v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider polynomial nonlinear PDEs on compact manifolds with finite-dimensional forcing terms. We provide necessary and sufficient conditions under which the forcing, through the nonlinear dynamics, attains a dense subspace on manifolds with and without boundary. Our key argument is Nachbin's theorem, which is an analogue of the well-known Stone-Weierstrass theorem in spaces of differentiable functions. As applications, we prove small-time approximate controllability by additive finite-dimensional controls, topological irreducibility, and almost sure unboundedness of Sobolev norms.
item.dc:creator: R\'emi Buffe, Alessandro Duca, Hugo Parada

item.title: Preventing Model Extraction in Contextual Linear Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.29918v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Consider a contextual linear optimization problem, where a predict-then-optimize (PTO) system returns optimal decisions without revealing the cost vectors used in its downstream linear program. Our focus is on how to prevent attackers, who can submit context queries, from extracting the underlying prediction model. Although the cost-to-decision map is many-to-one, observations across contexts can reveal the underlying prediction model. For linear models, we provide sufficient conditions where the attacker can learn the model up to positive scaling by only observing the decision. These conditions motivate an adaptive attack that alternates inverse optimization with boundary sampling, i.e., using context queries leading to decision boundaries of the current attacker model. To prevent extraction, we propose a mechanism that perturbs decisions only when the predicted cost vector is near a decision boundary. We establish a regret bound in terms of the perturbation radius. For the attackers that fit the defended responses as optimal decisions under the evaluation distribution, we also prove a lower bound on expected extraction error. Experiments on synthetic instances and real data quantify the security-performance trade-off of the defense mechanism and illustrate that our defense can increase the extraction error.
item.dc:creator: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Tianyi Lin, Wenxuan Liu

item.title: Saturating spaces for the squared-gradient nonlinearity on compact Riemannian manifolds via Nash embeddings
item.description: arXiv:2610.29952v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the saturation property on smooth compact Riemannian manifolds without boundary. Starting from a finite-dimensional space of smooth functions, one considers successive iterations of the nonlinear map $f\mapsto|\nabla_g f|_g^2$ and convex combinations. We extend to the general setting of compact manifolds existing results on particular geometries, namely the torus, spheres and Lie groups. Our approach relies on the existence of an isometric embedding of the manifold into $\mathbb{R}^n$ due to Nash. As an application, we obtain global approximate controllability in arbitrarily small time for the bilinear Schr\"odinger equation on any connected compact Riemannian manifold, with finitely many potentials.
item.dc:creator: Buffe R\'emi, Duca Alessandro, Parada Hugo

item.title: Rigidity of the ball for Hartree-type energies and second shape derivative via a continuity argument
item.description: arXiv:2610.29958v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the second shape derivative of an optimal design functional involving a nonlocal term in order to prove rigidity of the ball. Our approach relies on a continuity argument that relates the second variation to that of the corresponding local problem. The model serves as a prototype for a broader class of shape optimization problems to which the same strategy may be adapted.
item.dc:creator: Dario Mazzoleni, Riccardo Moraschi, Berardo Ruffini

item.title: Facets of the X-ray polytope of doubly stochastic matrices
item.description: arXiv:2610.30058v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the polytope of anti-diagonal X-rays of k x k doubly stochastic matrices, the image of the Birkhoff polytope under the map that sums the entries along each anti-diagonal. Its facets other than the coordinate facets are the minimal joint tail bounds for lattice laws of a sum of two dependent uniform random variables. We give an exact facet criterion in terms of the allowed edges of a tight graph. For rays of the underlying tropical fan, total support of the tight graph suffices for a facet but is not necessary, as an example with k=19 shows. Up to affine functions and positive scaling, the potentials that define a facet form a polytope whose vertices are its rays. Facets propagate by padding and by grid refinement under explicit hypotheses. We give infinite families of facets from no step potential, facets of quadratic height, superpolynomially many facets, and a classification of three-step potentials. Total support of a step potential is characterized by a Hall-type condition on block starts; with computer assistance, total support decides facets of step potentials for k<=26. The facet counts up to k=12 are found directly for k<=3 and, for k>=4, come from an enumeration by a provably complete algorithm; an independent exact recomputation reproduces its ray lists for 5<=k<=12.
item.dc:creator: Prashant Chaudhary, Kapil Khandelwal

item.title: Parallel AI Agent Collaboration as Graph-Structured Distributed Block Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.30074v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Parallel AI agents can produce useful local edits yet degrade a shared solution when their edits are combined. We model this coordination problem as discrete block optimization with an exactly evaluable objective and a known dependency graph. Independent sets certify compatible edits whose verified gains, measured against the same current solution, add exactly. A coordinator constructs a safe compatible candidate and can also evaluate interacting edits to capture favorable interactions. We prove that an optimal fractional coloring yields a merger that preserves a $1/\chi_f(G)$ fraction of the total verified local improvement, where $\chi_f(G)$ is the graph's fractional chromatic number. This guarantee is tight among mergers that select a subset of the same proposals. Under conditional local-improvement guarantees and a block error-bound condition, repeated collaboration converges geometrically in the objective gap. The rate separates task structure, agent allocation, and computation cost, yielding a linear program for agent assignment and an explicit time-cost trade-off. Code-repair experiments show that verified merging resolves conflicts between individually useful edits that cause naive merging to fail. On larger conflict-free tasks, parallel agents reduce modeled completion time at higher input-token-equivalent cost. On three public road networks, fractional integration retains 922 units of verified graph-cut improvement across 90 paired runs. For route-search agents sharing exclusive access to vehicle routes, fractional scheduling reduces measured wall time by a median of 15% across twelve paired runs, with route-cost changes varying across runs.
item.dc:creator: Hanmin Li, Yury Demidovich, Peter Richt\'arik

item.title: A Quasipolynomial Algorithm for $\ell_\infty$ Contractions
item.description: arXiv:2610.30122v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give an algorithm for computing an $\eps$-approximate fixed point of any $d$-dimensional nonexpansion with respect to the $\ell_\infty$ norm in time $\log(1/\eps)^{O(\log^2 d)}$. At its core, our method uses a boosting argument to geometrically shrink a search region. Among other consequences, our algorithm implies that simple stochastic games can be solved in quasipolynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Ashkan Soleymani, Gabriele Farina

item.title: Port-Hamiltonian systems with energy and power ports
item.description: arXiv:2405.01241v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We extend the port-Hamiltonian framework defined with respect to a Lagrangian submanifold and a Dirac structure by augmenting the Lagrangian submanifold with the space of external variables. The new pair of conjugated variables is called energy port. We show that in the most general case, the extension describes constrained Hamiltonian systems whose Hamiltonian function depends on inputs.
item.dc:creator: Kaja Krhac, Bernhard Maschke, Arjan van der Schaft

item.title: An Inexact Variable Metric Proximal Gradient-subgradient Algorithm for a Class of Fractional Optimization Problems
item.description: arXiv:2504.11023v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we study a class of fractional optimization problems, in which the numerator of the objective is the sum of a convex function and a differentiable function with a Lipschitz continuous gradient, while the denominator is a nonsmooth convex function. This model captures ratio-type formulations arising in sparse learning and related applications. To address this class of problems, we propose an inexact variable metric proximal gradient-subgradient algorithm (iVPGSA), which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first inexact proximal algorithm specifically designed for such type of fractional problems. By incorporating a variable metric proximal term and allowing for approximate subproblem solutions under a flexible error criterion, the proposed algorithm is highly adaptable to a broader range of problems while achieving favorable computational efficiency. Under suitable assumptions, we establish that any accumulation point of the generated sequence is a critical point of the target problem. Moreover, we develop a Kurdyka-{\L}ojasiewicz (KL)-based analysis framework, relying only on the classical KL property and its associated exponent, to prove the global convergence of the entire sequence and characterize its convergence rate, \textit{without} requiring a strict sufficient descent property. Our results clarify how the classical KL exponent and inexactness jointly influence the convergence rate. Finally, numerical experiments on the $\ell_1/\ell_2$ Lasso problem and the constrained $\ell_1/\ell_2$ sparse optimization problem demonstrate the computational advantages of the iVPGSA over existing representative algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Lei Yang, Xiangrui Kong, Min Zhang, Yaohua Hu

item.title: Variational structure of Fokker-Planck equations with variable mobility
item.description: arXiv:2505.10676v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study Fokker--Planck equations with symmetric, positive definite mobility matrices capturing diffusion in heterogeneous environments. A weighted Wasserstein metric is introduced for which these equations are gradient flows. This metric is shown to emerge from an optimal control problem in the space of probability densities for a class of variable mobility matrices, with the cost function capturing the work dissipated via friction. Using the Nash-Kuiper isometric embedding theorem for Riemannian manifolds, we demonstrate the existence of optimal transport maps. Additionally, we construct a time-discrete variational scheme, establish key properties for the associated minimizing problem, and prove convergence to weak solutions of the associated Fokker-Planck equation.
item.dc:creator: Hailiang Liu, Athanasios E. Tzavaras

item.title: Stackelberg stopping games
item.description: arXiv:2507.19746v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a Stackelberg variant of the classical discrete-time Dynkin game, in which Player 1 (the leader) commits to a stopping strategy first and Player 2 (the follower) responds optimally. This leader-follower structure induces an optimal control problem for the leader and gives rise to intrinsic time-inconsistency. We first clarify notions of precommitment and equilibrium strategies in the Stackelberg setting, and contrast them with the Nash equilibrium in the standard Dynkin game using a finite-horizon example. We then consider an infinite-horizon framework with a time-homogeneous Markov process on a general Polish state space. We characterize the leader's value function under randomized precommitment strategies and show that randomized exact equilibrium strategies may fail to exist via a counterexample. Motivated by this nonexistence phenomenon, we introduce an entropy-regularized Stackelberg stopping game. The regularization induces a continuous response rule and yields the existence of randomized regular equilibria. We further show that these regular equilibria induce epsilon-equilibria for the original Stackelberg stopping game when the regularization parameter is sufficiently small. In the finite-state setting, we also establish a limiting result as the regularization parameter converges to zero.
item.dc:creator: Jingjie Zhang, Zhou Zhou

item.title: Data-Driven Hull-Fouling Cleaning Schedule Optimization to Reduce Carbon Footprint of Vessels
item.description: arXiv:2602.11248v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In response to climate change, the International Maritime Organization has introduced regulations to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping. Compliance with these regulations is increasingly expected from individual shipping companies and can be achieved through more frequent hull and propeller cleanings. Since this maintenance work entails high costs, vessel operators are confronted with the trade-off between lower fleet emissions and better economic performance. As a result, assessing whether fuel efficiency has declined sufficiently to warrant cleaning from an environmental and economic standpoint is a critical task. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel dynamic-programming-based algorithm to optimize vessel cleaning schedules. The main components of the optimization problem are a data-driven function for the fuel consumption costs and an additive term that sums up the costs per vessel cleaning. In numerical experiments, we demonstrate the usefulness of our proposed methodology based on real-world sensor data from nine tramp trading vessels. The results confirm that, over four years, fuel consumption can be reduced by up to 5%, even when accounting for the costs of the additional cleaning events.
item.dc:creator: Samuel J. Ward, Marah-Lisanne Thormann, Julian Wharton, Alain Zemkoho

item.title: Fast Relax-and-Round Unit Commitment with Economic Horizons
item.description: arXiv:2603.15934v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The US energy system is under increasing pressure to serve expanding data centers loads and to accommodate a larger number of generating units with varying technologies and ownership structures. Therefore, developing new unit commitment (UC) methods remains a priority for reliable and affordable grid operations. We expand our novel computational method for UC to include ramping constraints and long-horizon planning, and provide a theoretical bound on its accuracy. We solve problems with thousands of generators at 5-minute market intervals. We show that our method can solve UC problems with over 20,000 generators in approximately 10 seconds on commodity hardware and that an increased planning horizon leads to sizable op- erational cost savings. This is twice as fast as the leading commercial solver, Gurobi. The gap increases when adding more constraints. Our method can be implemented using existing continuous optimization solvers and adapted for different applications. We prove a bound on the error of these solvers and show that it vanishes (in relative terms) as the problem becomes larger. Our novel algorithm could allow an operator to make horizon-aware economic decisions for large systems.
item.dc:creator: Shaked Regev, Evan J. R. Brody, Charles Foltz, Eve Tsybina, Slaven Peles

item.title: An Inexact Trust-Region Method for Structured Nonsmooth Optimization with Application to Risk-Averse Stochastic Programming
item.description: arXiv:2604.07216v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a trust-region method for efficiently minimizing the sum of a smooth function, a nonsmooth convex function, and the composition of a convex Lipschitz continuous function with a smooth function. Optimization problems with this structure arise in numerous applications including risk-averse stochastic programming and subproblems for nonsmooth penalty nonlinear programming methods. Our algorithm permits the use of inexact value and derivative information, enabling the solution of infinite-dimensional problems governed by, e.g., partial differential equations (PDEs). We prove global convergence of our method and under additional regularity assumptions, demonstrate that the sequence of iterates accumulates at a stationary point of our target problem. We demonstrate our method's efficiency on two PDE-constrained optimization examples, showing that its performance is invariant to the PDE discretization size.
item.dc:creator: Drew P. Kouri

item.title: Benchmarking Bilevel Derivative-Free Optimization Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2605.30531v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bilevel optimization involves an upper-level and a lower-level decision maker. The lower-level optimization problem is nested within the constraints of the upper-level one. A point is said to be admissible for the bilevel problem if it satisfies all constraints and is optimal for the lower-level decision-maker. Bilevel derivative-free optimization (BL-DFO) algorithms address bilevel optimization problems in which the upper-level is solved using a derivative-free optimization method, and an inexact method it used to solve the lower- level. In this context, existing BL-DFO benchmarking techniques often do not rigorously validate the admissibility of proposed solutions, and do not adequately account for the computational effort deployed by the upper- and lower-level solvers. This work proposes a benchmarking methodology for BL-DFO algorithms. A post-optimization procedure, named the refereeing procedure, is introduced to discard non-admissible points and ensures a fair comparison between the algorithms. The computational effort deployed by upper- and lower-level solvers is also taken into account into the overall computational cost. Numerical experiments illustrate the benchmarking methodology.
item.dc:creator: Charles Audet, Valentin Dijon, Youssef Diouane

item.title: Signature Methods for Optimal Market Making
item.description: arXiv:2606.19772v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a signature-based method to solve the optimal market-making problem under a mean-variance criterion. By exploiting signature linearization techniques, we reduce the market-making problem to a pseudo-linear optimization over the expected signature of an augmented market path, and we develop a signature algorithm named Sig-REINFORCE to learn the optimal bid and ask quotes. We test our method in two scenarios, in which market-order arrivals follow either a Poisson or a self-exciting Hawkes process, and we benchmark it against a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) baseline.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Gennaro, Thibaut Mastrolia, Francesca Primavera

item.title: Strategic Index Reconstitution: Differential Games, Closed-Loop Equilibria and Mean-Field Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2609.15901v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a continuous-time, multiasset trading game around index reconstitution, in which opportunistic traders have heterogeneous beliefs about the future index constitution and interact through transient cross-asset price impact and instantaneous execution costs. Opportunistic traders build inventory based on their individual beliefs about the future index constitution before a public announcement, adjust their positions to the revealed composition, and unwind them against the indexer's prescribed rebalancing trades at the implementation date when the new index composition takes effect. Under a no-price-manipulation condition, we construct a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium. Its affine feedback policies are computed from a non-standard matrix Riccati equation and linear ODEs whose number and dimensions are independent of population size. Under mean-field scaling, we construct a mean-field equilibrium and obtain quantitative convergence and approximate-Nash bounds. Numerical illustrations show that greater competition among opportunists dampens price swings around implementation and that opportunistic trading lowers the indexer's implementation shortfall unless price resilience is very low. Holding the average belief fixed, greater belief dispersion can increase gross trading volume without changing net aggregate opportunist holdings or price impact.
item.dc:creator: Lukas-Benedikt Fiechtner, Jose Blanchet

item.title: Entrywise nonnegativity of the inverse relative gain array in dimension six
item.description: arXiv:2609.35558v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove that $(G\circ G^{-1})^{-1}$ is entrywise nonnegative for every real symmetric positive definite matrix $G$ of order at most six. Its entries are strictly positive exactly within the connected components of the nonzero-entry graph of $G$. An explicit rational example of order seven establishes sharpness. We give two complementary structural proofs. The analytic proof combines a trace obstruction with continuation of positive column forms and a bordering identity. The algebraic proof establishes a stronger four-dimensional polarized inequality through an explicit ten-square polynomial certificate. A common framework relates biquadratic positivity, column forms, positive semidefinite precision loads, and inverse relative gain array nonnegativity in consecutive dimensions. Further consequences include exact load-deficit identities, polynomial sum-of-squares certificates with the covariance fixed, and a reverse Schur--Horn majorization inequality with the same sharp dimension bound. In every dimension, sufficiently large powers of the inverse relative gain array are doubly stochastic.
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Uhlmann, Jie Wang

item.title: Rank-sensitive vertex bounds for semidefinite lifts
item.description: arXiv:2610.04498v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study how the ranks of factors in a positive semidefinite slack factorization constrain its size. We bound the number of low-rank vertex factors in any fixed factorization, and use this to determine the asymptotic order of the minimum factorization size under any fixed bound on vertex-factor ranks: $\Theta(n\log n)$ for permutahedra $\Pi_n$ and $\Theta(\log N)$ for regular $N$-gons. In the rank-one case this gives the order of the minimum dimension of a space of real functions on the vertices in which every facet slack is a sum of squares, with no symmetry or degree restriction. For unrestricted lifts, the bound gives $\mathrm{xc}_{\mathrm{PSD}}(\Pi_n)\ge n+\log_3 n-O(1)$, and shows that a permutahedron factorization of linear size would need vertex factors of rank $\Omega(\log n)$ at all but a vanishing fraction of vertices. We also prove that every polytope of real positive semidefinite rank at most four has at most twelve vertices, and construct explicit size-four lifts for every square-symmetric octagon, so eight is attained. The upper bound combines a count of the polygon corners reached by curves of rank-one factors with incidence constraints on factor ranks. Whether eight is the maximum remains open.
item.dc:creator: Avinash Bhardwaj

item.title: A continuous-time limit for particle swarm optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.07373v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a popular class of gradient-free methods for global optimization. We study a continuous-time model for momentum-free PSO with personal-best memory and global-best interaction. Unlike previous models which rely on smooth approximations, we keep the original discontinuous personal- and global-best processes. We study the small-step limit and show that weak limit points satisfy a stochastic differential inclusion: personal-best variables obey a relaxed record condition, while fast switching of the global-best selector leads to a convexified interaction. We then give conditions under which the true original selectors are recovered. Under suitable regularity and nondegeneracy assumptions, Brownian noise allows us to identify the personal-best processes with the latest record positions of the limiting trajectories and to prove that the particle attaining the global best is unique at almost every time. The resulting continuous-time dynamics retain both selection rules without smoothing them.
item.dc:creator: Pascal Bianchi, Radu-Alexandru Dragomir, Yerkin Yesbay

item.title: Dual-Inertial Bregman Methods with Energy-Based Safeguarding
item.description: arXiv:2610.20420v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop dual-inertial Bregman proximal methods for convex optimization and analyze their convergence through an exact signed-drift representation. For unrestarted iterations, one-sided directional curvature control yields a last-iterate $\cO((1+\log k)/k^2)$ rate, improving to $\cO(k^{-2})$ under weighted summability. A computable energy-based safeguard guarantees a global $\cO(N^{-1})$ objective-gap bound, counting all proximal oracle calls. Under a stepsize condition and local quadratic growth with suitable kernel regularity, the safeguarded methods restart finitely and eventually converge linearly. Numerical experiments illustrate the methods on entropy regression and nonnegative least squares.
item.dc:creator: Kangming Chen

item.title: Dynamic Programming for Value-at-Risk Markov Decision Processes in Continuous Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.24439v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Value-at-Risk (VaR) is a widely adopted quantile-based risk measure in practice, yet incorporating VaR objectives into Markov decision processes (VaR MDPs) remains a longstanding challenge. Recent work has derived dynamic programming equations for VaR MDPs in finite state and action spaces but left the case of more general spaces unresolved. This paper establishes, for the first time, the validity of these equations in continuous spaces, for both finite- and infinite-horizon settings. Such cases naturally arise in many real-world dynamic decision-making problems. As an application, we study an optimal execution problem with a VaR objective and demonstrate that our framework enables the characterization of optimal dynamic strategies, resolving an open question in the field.
item.dc:creator: Xian Chen, Erick Delage, Weikai Wang

item.title: Kurdyka-{\L}ojasiewicz-based convergence analysis with approximate weakly convex subdifferentials: bundle, quadratic penalty, and moving balls approximation methods
item.description: arXiv:2610.26263v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz (KL) property has been widely used for establishing global sequential convergence and analyzing local convergence rate of optimization algorithms. Most existing analysis frameworks rely on the construction of a suitable KL potential function such that along the sequence generated, it admits sufficient descents and its exact subdifferentials are suitably controlled by successive changes of the iterates. Nevertheless, a handful of important algorithms, such as bundle methods and quadratic penalty methods, are not known to have potential functions verifying the aforementioned properties, rendering their convergence analysis out of the reach of existing KL-based convergence analysis template. In this paper, we develop a new convergence analysis framework to extend the applicability of KL-based analysis. Our framework is built on a weakly convex KL potential function $\psi$. It allows approximate sufficient descents, the use of diminishing stepsizes, and controls on enlarged subdifferentials of $\psi$ known as the $\varrho$-weakly-convex-$\varepsilon$-subdifferentials. We illustrate the usefulness of our framework by establishing the global sequential convergence and analyzing the local convergence rate of some recent variants of bundle method, quadratic penalty method and moving balls approximation method. Specifically, we show that these methods fall under our framework by presenting explicit and natural choices of $\psi$, and derive suitable choices of model parameters, penalty parameters and constraint shrinkage parameters, respectively, for establishing their global sequential convergence and local convergence rate based on the KL property and exponent of $\psi$.
item.dc:creator: Jiefeng Xu, Guoyin Li, Ting Kei Pong

item.title: When Weak Submodularity Meets Matroids: How Does Standard Greedy Behave?
item.description: arXiv:2610.26967v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Weakly submodular maximization finds numerous applications in machine learning, data mining and statistics. In particular, under a cardinality constraint, the standard greedy algorithm is known to attain the tight $(1-e^{-\gamma})$-approximation guarantee, where $\gamma$ denotes the submodularity ratio. However, when considering general matroid constraints, \emph{how well standard greedy can perform} has remained a longstanding open question. In this paper, we resolve this question by studying the worst-case approximation guarantee $R_{\mathrm{gr}}(\gamma,r)$ of standard forward greedy, where $r$ is the rank of matroid. Specifically, our first contribution is the following refined lower bound \begin{equation*} R_{gr}(\gamma,r)\ge \max\left\{ \frac{\gamma}{r}, \frac{\gamma^2} {B_\gamma+\sqrt{\gamma(r-1)}}, \frac{\gamma^{r+1}} {2-\gamma+\gamma^{r+1}}, \frac{\gamma^2} {14\left(B_\gamma+\sqrt{\gamma(1-\gamma)(r-1)}\right)} \right\}, \end{equation*} where $B_\gamma\triangleq2-\gamma+\gamma^2$. This lower bound not only strictly improves upon the previous guarantee of $0.4\gamma^2/(1+\sqrt{\gamma r})$, but also can recover the classical $1/2$-approximation guarantee at $\gamma=1$. Subsequently, a corresponding upper bound is established for $R_{\mathrm{gr}}(\gamma,r)$, namely, \begin{equation}\label{eq_upper_abstract} R_{gr}(\gamma,r) \le\min\left\{\frac{1}{2},20\max\left\{\frac{\gamma}{r}, \frac{\gamma^2}{B_\gamma+ \sqrt{\gamma(1-\gamma)(r-1)}}\right\}\right\}. \end{equation} For every fixed $\gamma\in(0,1)$, this equation effectively sharpens the recent $O_\gamma(1/\log(n-1))$ upper bound to $O_\gamma(r^{-1/2})$, where $n$ is the size of ground set. Putting all these results together, we eventually can obtain \[R_{gr}(\gamma,r) = \Theta\left( \max\left\{\frac{\gamma}{r}, \frac{\gamma^2} {1+\sqrt{\gamma(1-\gamma)r}}\right\} \right).\]
